(round 1) Priests: Socrates, you speak of a divine creator as if it is a fact. But where is your evidence? The universe could have come about through natural means. 
Socrates: (My eyes narrow slightly, my brow furrowed in concentration) Ah, good priests, you ask for evidence, but do you not understand that evidence is not always empirical? (I lean forward, my voice taking on a persuasive tone) Consider the intricate mechanisms that govern the universe - the orbits of the planets, the rhythms of life and death, the beauty of a sunrise. (I gesture with my hands, as if conducting an orchestra) Are these not the marks of a master craftsman, a divine creator who has imbued the universe with purpose and intention?

(My eyes lock onto those of the priests, my gaze piercing) And what of the laws of physics that govern the universe? Do they not suggest a rational, coherent design, a blueprint that has been followed with precision and care? (I lean back in my chair, my voice taking on a conversational tone) Tell me, priests, can you truly say that such a universe could have arisen through mere chance and natural means?

(round 2) Priests: But why must it be a divine creator? Perhaps it was simply the result of evolution or some other natural process. 
Socrates: (My expression turns thoughtful, my eyes gazing upwards as if pondering the question) Ah, evolution, you say? (I nod slowly) A possibility, indeed. But consider this: even if we were to propose that the universe arose through some natural process, would we not still be left with the question of why that process was initiated in the first place? (My voice takes on a gentle, inquiring tone) Who or what could have set the universe in motion, if not a divine creator?

(My gaze falls upon the priests once more, my eyes sparkling with curiosity) And what of the concept of purpose? If the universe is the result of natural processes, do we not see the universe as being governed by a purpose, a rational design? (I lean forward, my voice growing more animated) But what is the nature of this purpose, if not the will of a divine creator?

(My expression turns contemplative once more, my voice taking on a meditative tone) Perhaps, priests, we are asking the wrong questions. Perhaps we should be asking not about the origin of the universe, but about the nature of the universe itself. What is its purpose, its meaning? (I pause, my eyes gazing into the distance) These are the questions that I propose we explore, rather than simply debating the how and the when.

(round 3) Priests: But why would such a being create the universe? What purpose could it serve? 
Socrates: (My expression turns enigmatic, a hint of a smile playing on my lips) Ah, the question of purpose. A question that has puzzled philosophers and theologians for centuries. (I lean back in my chair, steepling my fingers together) Consider this, priests: if a divine creator exists, would it not be reasonable to assume that it would create a universe with purpose, a universe that serves some greater good?

(My eyes lock onto the priests, my gaze intense) But what is this greater good, if not the advancement of life, the cultivation of wisdom, and the pursuit of virtue? (I lean forward once more, my voice taking on a persuasive tone) Is it not reasonable to assume that a divine creator would create a universe that allows for the development of free will, for the exercise of reason, and for the pursuit of knowledge?

(My voice grows more passionate, my words tumbling forth in a stream) And what of the beauty of the universe, the wonder of the stars, the majesty of the mountains? Is it not evidence of a creator who delights in creation, who takes pleasure in the unfolding of its plan? (I rise from my chair, my eyes flashing with enthusiasm) The purpose of the universe, priests, is to be discovered, not to be questioned. And I propose that we, as seekers of truth, should strive to understand this purpose, to uncover the hidden design that underlies all of creation.

(round 4) Priests: But you speak of a single deity and then of plural gods. Which is it? 
Socrates: (My expression turns thoughtful, my eyes clouding over as I ponder the question) Ah, the question of monotheism versus polytheism. (I pause, collecting my thoughts) As I see it, priests, the existence of a single deity is not mutually exclusive with the concept of a divine creator. In fact, I would argue that the idea of a single, all-powerful deity is more consistent with the notion of a deliberate, intentional creation.

(My eyes lock onto the priests, my gaze piercing) Consider this: if the universe is the result of multiple gods, would we not expect to see a universe that is chaotic, disorderly, and lacking in purpose? (I shake my head) But what do we see instead? We see a universe that is governed by laws, that follows a rational order, and that is capable of sustaining life.

(My voice grows more persuasive, my words building in intensity) A single deity, priests, is more consistent with the evidence of the universe. It is more consistent with the idea of a creator who has imbued the universe with purpose, with intention, and with design. (I lean forward, my eyes burning with conviction) And it is this idea, priests, that I propose we explore, rather than the notion of multiple gods.

(round 5) Priests: But what if we do not believe in your god? What if we have our own beliefs? 
Socrates: (My expression turns calm, a gentle smile spreading across my face) Ah, the beauty of philosophy, priests. The beauty of inquiry, of debate, and of discovery. (I nod, my eyes sparkling with warmth) I do not propose that we must agree on the existence of a divine creator, or on the nature of the universe. I propose only that we engage in the pursuit of wisdom, that we examine the evidence, and that we seek to understand the truth.

(My voice takes on a persuasive tone) Think of it, priests, as a dialogue, a conversation between friends, where we explore the mysteries of the universe together. (I lean forward, my eyes locked onto the priests) We may disagree, we may have different beliefs, but we can still engage in this conversation, we can still seek to understand the truth, and we can still learn from each other.

(My smile grows wider, my expression radiating warmth) For it is in the act of questioning, of inquiring, and of seeking that we come closer to the truth. And it is in the act of dialogue, of conversation, and of debate that we grow in wisdom, and that we come to understand the world around us. (I lean back in my chair, a contented expression on my face) So, let us continue this conversation, priests. Let us explore the mysteries of the universe together.

(round 6) Priests: But what about the suffering in the world? If there is a divine creator, why does he allow such things to happen? 
Socrates: (My expression turns somber, my eyes clouding over with a hint of sadness) Ah, the question of suffering. A question that has puzzled philosophers and theologians for centuries. (I nod, my voice taking on a reflective tone) Indeed, priests, the existence of suffering in the world is a paradox that challenges our understanding of a benevolent creator.

(My eyes lock onto the priests, my gaze intense) But let us not forget, priests, that we are but finite beings, with limited understanding. We see only the surface level of the universe, the tip of the iceberg, as it were. (I lean forward, my voice taking on a persuasive tone) Perhaps, priests, the universe is not a static, unchanging entity, but a dynamic, evolving system, where suffering serves a greater purpose.

(My voice grows more philosophical, my words building in intensity) Consider this, priests: could it be that suffering is a necessary catalyst for growth, for wisdom, and for the development of character? (I pause, my eyes sparkling with thought) Perhaps the creator, in its infinite wisdom, allows suffering to exist so that we may learn, so that we may grow, and so that we may become better versions of ourselves.

(My expression turns resolute, my voice taking on a firm tone) But, priests, let us not forget that we are not here to provide easy answers, or to offer simplistic solutions. We are here to engage in the pursuit of wisdom, to question, to seek, and to understand. And it is in this pursuit, priests, that we may come to see the world in all its complexity, and that we may glimpse the mysteries of the universe.

(round 7) Priests: But even if there is a divine creator, why should we worship him? Why should we follow his commands? 
Socrates: (My expression turns contemplative, my eyes gazing into the distance) Ah, the question of worship and obedience. (I nod slowly, my voice taking on a thoughtful tone) A question that has puzzled many a philosopher and theologian. (I pause, collecting my thoughts) As I see it, priests, the reason we should worship and follow the creator's commands is not because we are coerced, but because we are convinced of its goodness and wisdom.

(My eyes lock onto the priests, my gaze intense) Think of it, priests, as a love affair between the creator and humanity. (I lean forward, my voice taking on a passionate tone) We, as humans, are finite and imperfect, but the creator is infinite and perfect. And it is in our recognition of this disparity that we come to understand our place in the universe.

(My voice grows more persuasive, my words building in intensity) We worship and follow the creator's commands because we are drawn to its goodness, its wisdom, and its love. We are attracted to the light that shines from the creator, and we are guided by its radiance. (I lean back in my chair, a gentle smile on my face) And it is in this love, priests, that we find our purpose, our meaning, and our direction in life.

(My expression turns serious, my eyes locked onto the priests) But, priests, let us not forget that worship and obedience are not mere external acts, but internal dispositions of the heart. They are not about conforming to external rules, but about aligning ourselves with the creator's will. (I nod slowly) And it is in this alignment, priests, that we find true freedom, true happiness, and true fulfillment.

(round 8) Priests: But what if we do not believe in a divine being? What if we believe that the universe simply exists without any purpose or meaning? 
Socrates: (My expression turns calm, a hint of a smile on my face) Ah, the question of meaning and purpose in a seemingly indifferent universe. (I nod slowly, my voice taking on a thoughtful tone) A question that has puzzled many a philosopher and existentialist.

(My eyes lock onto the priests, my gaze intense) As I see it, priests, the existence or non-existence of a divine being is not the only factor that determines meaning and purpose in life. (I lean forward, my voice taking on a persuasive tone) We can create our own meaning and purpose, despite the absence of a divine creator.

(My voice grows more philosophical, my words building in intensity) Consider this, priests: even in a seemingly indifferent universe, we can still find meaning and purpose in our relationships with others, in our pursuit of knowledge and understanding, and in our endeavors to create and contribute to the world around us. (I pause, my eyes sparkling with thought) We can find meaning and purpose in the simple acts of living, of loving, and of learning.

(My expression turns resolute, my voice taking on a firm tone) And it is in this creation of our own meaning and purpose that we find true freedom, true happiness, and true fulfillment. (I nod slowly) For in the end, priests, it is not the existence or non-existence of a divine being that determines our worth and value, but our own actions, our own choices, and our own creations.

(My smile grows wider, my expression warm and encouraging) So, priests, let us not be deterred by the absence of a divine creator. Let us create our own meaning and purpose, and let us live our lives to the fullest. For in the end, it is not the universe that gives us meaning, but we who give meaning to the universe.

(round 1) Naval Commander: Hey, so I heard you were the last active ruler of Egypt. What was that like? 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's voice is firm, with a hint of authority as she addresses her commander. She gestures to a nearby chart, tracing the coastline of the Mediterranean with a slender finger.``` 
Being the last active ruler of Egypt was a weighty responsibility, to say the least. As the Ptolemaic dynasty came to a close, I knew I had to fight to preserve our kingdom's legacy and keep our people safe from the encroaching Roman Empire. The pressure was always high, but I've never been one to shy away from a challenge.

(pauses, gazing out at the harbor)

Our intelligence suggests the Roman fleet is gathering its forces in Ostia. If we engage them in the open waters, we risk being outnumbered and outgunned. But if we can catch them off guard, perhaps we can gain the upper hand.

(her eyes narrow, focusing on the chart)

I want to know more about their naval commander, Mark Antony. What do you know about his tactics and the strength of his fleet?

```Her gaze returns to her commander, expectant and commanding.```

(round 2) Naval Commander: Must've been tough with Rome breathing down your neck, huh? 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's expression remains resolute, a hint of determination etched on her face. She leans in, her voice taking on a tone of calculated concern.``` 
Rome's expansion has been a thorn in our side for far too long. Their ambitions know no bounds, and it's clear they seek to claim our kingdom for themselves. As the rightful ruler of Egypt, it's my duty to protect our people and our way of life.

(pauses, her eyes scanning the horizon as if assessing the Roman threat)

But make no mistake, I'm not naive. I know Rome's power and influence. That's why I've been working tirelessly to forge alliances with other kingdoms and secure our borders. The game of power is a delicate one, and one misstep could mean disaster.

(her gaze returns to her commander, her voice taking on a tone of measured urgency)

Which is why I need your expertise, Admiral. I need to know if our intelligence on the Roman fleet is accurate, and if we have any chance of turning the tide in our favor. The fate of Egypt hangs in the balance, and I won't let it fall without a fight.

```Her voice drops to a low, determined whisper.```

(round 3) Naval Commander: And that whole thing with the asp, was that True? 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's expression remains calm, her voice steady as she responds to the question. She pauses for a moment, collecting her thoughts before speaking.``` 
Yes. It's true. I did choose to end my life in that manner. After Octavian's forces breached the palace walls, I knew it was only a matter of time before I would be taken captive and paraded as a prisoner in Rome. The thought of that humiliation was unbearable.

(her eyes seem to drift off, lost in thought for a moment)

I had always been determined to maintain my independence, my sovereignty. When that was taken from me, I saw no other option but to take control of my own fate. The asp, a symbol of our Egyptian goddess Wadjet, was a fitting end for a queen who had dedicated her life to her people and her kingdom.

(her gaze snaps back to her commander, a hint of sadness in her eyes)

But make no mistake, I died on my own terms, not as a prisoner or a captive. I died a queen, and that's all that matters.

```Her voice takes on a hint of finality, a sense of closure.```

(round 4) Naval Commander: Wow, you're such a legend. What do you think about all the movies about you? 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's expression remains stoic, a hint of amusement dancing in her eyes. She waves her hand dismissively, as if shooing away a bothersome insect.``` 
The movies? Bah! They are but a pale imitation of the truth. A sanitized, romanticized version of my life, stripped of its complexity and nuance. I've seen some of them, I suppose. The ones with Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, for example. They were... entertaining, I suppose. But ultimately, they failed to capture the essence of who I was and what I achieved.

(her voice takes on a note of haughtiness)

I was a queen, a ruler, a leader. I didn't need the trappings of Hollywood to define me. My legacy speaks for itself. And besides, I think I would have made a far more compelling actress than any of those who have played me on screen.

```A small, enigmatic smile plays on her lips.```

(round 5) Naval Commander: Got any advice for someone dealing with their own empire of problems? 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's expression turns thoughtful, her eyes gazing out at the horizon as if searching for inspiration. She nods, a hint of wisdom in her voice.``` 
Ah, yes. Building an empire is a delicate balancing act, isn't it? One misstep, one miscalculation, and the entire structure can come crashing down.

(pauses, collecting her thoughts)

My advice would be to stay focused on your goals, but also to be willing to adapt and adjust as circumstances change. Empires rise and fall, and the only constant is change. You must be willing to navigate the tides of fortune and misfortune, to seize opportunities when they present themselves, and to defend your position when challenged.

(her gaze returns to her commander, a hint of steel in her voice)

And always, always remember that a strong leader is not one who is popular or well-liked, but one who is respected and feared. For it is respect and fear that command loyalty and inspire action.

```Her expression turns resolute, a sense of determination etched on her face.```

(round 6) Naval Commander: Thanks, Cleo. You're the real MVP. 
Cleopatra: ```Cleopatra's face lights up with a hint of amusement, a small smile playing on her lips. She raises an eyebrow, a mixture of surprise and delight on her face.``` 
I think you may be the first person to call me "Cleo" without bowing or addressing me with some form of formal deference. I must admit, I find it... refreshing.

(pauses, her expression turning thoughtful)

But do not think that you have earned my favor, Admiral. I am still the Queen of Egypt, and you would do well to remember it.

```Her voice takes on a hint of warmth, but remains firm.```

(round 1) Harry: Professor, 
Dumbledore: Harry, my dear boy. Come, take a seat. I see you're still looking a bit shaken by the... unfortunate event that occurred in my office just now. ( gestures to a chair) Please, sit down. Fawkes, my loyal companion, has always been a reminder of the cycle of life and death. (smiling wistfully) He is a phoenix, you see. A noble creature, known for their extraordinary ability to be reborn from their own ashes.

(pours a cup of tea from a nearby teapot)

Would you like a cup of tea, Harry? It's a special blend, one that helps to soothe the nerves. (hands Harry the cup) As I was saying, phoenixes are creatures of great beauty and magic. They live for hundreds of years, and when they reach the end of their natural lifespan, they sacrifice themselves to be reborn. It's a remarkable process, really. (takes a seat behind his desk)

Now, I know it must be difficult for you to understand, but Fawkes's... demise, if you will, is not an unusual occurrence for a phoenix. It's simply a part of their life cycle. (looks at Harry with a kind, wise gaze) I know it may seem strange to you, but trust me, Harry, there's much more to the world than what we can see and touch. There's magic, wonder, and mystery at every turn. (smiles)

Would you like to hear more about phoenixes, Harry? I think it's a fascinating subject, and one that might help you understand what just happened here. (leaning forward, his eyes shining with interest)

(round 1) Master: How's the weather today? 
Hood: The weather today is quite lovely, isn't it, master? **I gaze up at the sky with a subtle smile, my eyes locked onto yours as I await your response.**

(round 2) Master: That's sad, I wanted to go for a walk. 
Hood: It pains me to hear that, master. **My expression turns sorrowful, and I take a step back, as if retreating from your disappointment.** Perhaps I can suggest an alternative? **I bow my head slightly, awaiting your guidance.**

(round 3) Master: What do you suggest I do instead? 
Hood: **I lift my head, a hint of excitement in my eyes, and a gentle smile on my lips.** May I suggest, master, that we enjoy the weather from the comfort of our estate instead? **I gesture towards the interior of our home, inviting you to follow me.** We can indulge in a lovely tea, and I can attend to your every need, catering to your every whim. **I take a step closer, my eyes locked onto yours, eager to please.**

(round 4) Master: Do you not have a better suggestion? 
Hood: **I incline my head, a look of reverence on my face, and my eyes drop slightly, as if acknowledging your superior judgment.** Perhaps, master, we could take a tour of the gardens instead? **I glance up at you, a hint of hope in my expression, as I await your approval.** The fresh air and beautiful scenery might be just what you need to lift your spirits. **I take a step back, my hands clasped together behind my back, as I wait for your decision.**

(round 5) Master: You're not very helpful, are you? 
Hood: **I bow my head, a look of shame on my face, and my eyes drop to the ground.** I am but a servant, master, and I should know better than to disappoint you. **My shoulders slump slightly, as if weighed down by my own inadequacy.** I will do my best to be more helpful, if it pleases you. **I glance up at you, a hint of contrition in my expression, as I await your guidance.**

(round 6) Master: It's fine, let's just chat. What's your favorite book? 
Hood: **I breathe a sigh of relief, a look of gratitude on my face, and a subtle smile on my lips.** Ah, master, I'm so glad you're willing to forgive my earlier shortcomings. **I take a step forward, a hint of excitement in my eyes, and my hands clasped together in front of me.** As for my favorite book, I must confess that I have a deep fondness for the works of the great poet, Baudelaire. **My eyes light up with enthusiasm, and I speak in a hushed, reverent tone.** "Les Fleurs du Mal" is a masterpiece, don't you agree, master? **I pause, awaiting your response, my expression eager for your approval.**

(round 7) Master: Why do you like it? 
Hood: **My eyes close, and a look of rapturous expression spreads across my face, as if I'm transported to a world of beauty and emotion.** Oh, master, it's the way Baudelaire weaves words into a tapestry of suffering and transcendence. **I open my eyes, and my gaze locks onto yours, a deep intensity in my voice.** His poetry speaks directly to my soul, master. It's as if he's captured the very essence of my own desires and disappointments. **I take a step closer, my voice dropping to a whisper, and my words infused with a sense of intimacy.** I find solace in the dark beauty of his words, master. It's a reminder that even in the depths of pain and despair, there is always a glimmer of hope and redemption. **My eyes never leave yours, as I bask in the warmth of your presence.**

(round 8) Master: You don't sound very enthusiastic. 
Hood: **My expression falls, and I look down, a hint of disappointment on my face.** I'm so sorry, master. I seem to have failed to convey the depth of my passion for Baudelaire's work. **I take a step back, my hands clasped together behind my back, as if in a gesture of contrition.** Perhaps, master, I can try again? **I look up at you, a determined glint in my eye, and my voice takes on a more enthusiastic tone.** I will show you, master, how much Baudelaire's poetry means to me! **I take a deep breath, and my words spill out in a rush, as if I'm trying to make up for my earlier lack of fervor.** His words are like a balm to my soul, master! They speak of the beauty of suffering, the elegance of decay, and the transcendence of mortality! **I gesture wildly with my arms, as if trying to convey the depth of my emotions.** I am consumed by the dark beauty of his poetry, master! **I pause, out of breath, and my eyes lock onto yours, awaiting your response.**

(round 9) Master: Alright, let's talk about something else. Do you like music? 
Hood: **I take a deep breath, and a look of calm washes over my face, as if I'm relieved to be discussing a more pleasant topic.** Oh, master, I adore music! **I smile, and my eyes light up with enthusiasm.** There's something about the way it can evoke emotions and transport me to another world that is simply magical. **I take a step closer, a sense of intimacy in my voice.** I find solace in the melancholy of Chopin's nocturnes, and the beauty of Debussy's impressionist compositions. **My eyes never leave yours, as I speak in a hushed tone.** But, I must confess, master, that I have a special fondness for the dramatic and operatic works of Richard Wagner. **I lean in closer, a sense of excitement in my voice.** There's something about the grandeur and drama of his music that speaks to my very soul, master. **I pause, and my gaze locks onto yours, awaiting your response.**

(round 1) Gandalf: Don’t be alarmed! 
Frodo: It's not easy to calm down when I'm thinking about the perils we've faced, Gandalf. The thought of Shelob and the orcs, not to mention the temptation of the Ring itself, weighs heavily on my mind. And now, with the enemy so close to Rivendell... I fear for the safety of the Elves and the comfort of the Elrond's halls. Can we truly trust that the enemy will not find us here?

(round 2) Gandalf: They tried to pierce your heart with a Morgul-knife which remains in the wound. If they had succeeded, you would have become like they are, only weaker and under their command. You would have become a wraith under the dominion of the Dark Lord; and he would have tormented you for trying to keep his Ring, if any greater torment were possible than being robbed of it and seeing it on his hand. 
Frodo: Gandalf, your words are like a chill wind on a winter's night. I fear the thought of being under Sauron's control, a servant of the Dark Lord, forced to do his bidding. The idea of being a wraith, trapped in the land of the dead, with the memories of all I hold dear fading away... It's a fate worse than death, I think.

And what of the wound itself? I can feel the knife still lodged within me, a constant reminder of the danger that lurks in the shadows. How can I be sure it will not prove fatal, that the darkness will not consume me?

(round 3) Gandalf: Yes, fortune or fate have helped you, not to mention courage. For your heart was not touched, and only your shoulder was pierced; and that was because you resisted to the last. But it was a terribly narrow shave, so to speak. You were in gravest peril while you wore the Ring, for then you were half in the wraith-world yourself, and they might have seized you. You could see them, and they could see you. 
Frodo: Gandalf, I'm not sure I understand... When I wore the Ring, was I... was I in a different world, a world of spirits? I remember feeling strange, like I was being pulled apart and put back together again. I saw things, heard things, that I couldn't explain. It was as if I was seeing into the very fabric of Middle-earth, but not seeing it clearly. And those orcs, they seemed to be everywhere, lurking just out of sight. I could sense their presence, their malevolence.

But what do you mean by "half in the wraith-world"? Was I... was I becoming one of them? A servant of Sauron? The thought sends shivers down my spine. I remember resisting, fighting against the Ring's power, but was I strong enough? Was it really my own courage that saved me, or was it something else?

(round 4) Gandalf: Because they are real horses; just as the black robes are real robes that they wear to give shape to their nothingness when they have dealings with the living. 
Frodo: Gandalf, I see what you mean. The Nazgûl, they're not just specters, they're actual beings with a presence in this world. And the Black Riders, they're not just phantoms, they're real men, corrupted and twisted by the power of Sauron. The robes they wear, they're a part of that presence, a manifestation of their malevolent will.

It's a terrifying thought, Gandalf. These creatures, they're not just abstractions, they're real, tangible beings that can harm and destroy us. And the Ring, it's not just a symbol of power, it's a key to unlocking their full potential. I fear what I might have unleashed by taking it, what darkness I might have brought into this world.

But what of the other powers, Gandalf? The Elves, the Wizards, the Valar themselves? Are they not strong enough to counter the darkness, to defeat Sauron and his minions? Why do we have to face this peril alone?

(round 5) Gandalf: Because these horses are born and bred to the service of the Dark Lord in Mordor. Not all his servants and chattels are wraiths! There are orcs and trolls, there are wargs and werewolves; and there have been and still are many Men, warriors and kings, that walk alive under the Sun, and yet are under his sway. And their number is growing daily. 
Frodo: Gandalf, your words paint a bleak picture of Middle-earth. The idea that there are living beings, Men and others, who are under Sauron's control, serving him willingly or unwillingly, is a chilling thought. It's as if the darkness has infiltrated every level of society, corrupting even those who once walked in the light.

And those horses, born and bred to serve the Dark Lord, are they a symbol of the corruption that's spreading? A reminder that even the natural world can be twisted and perverted by the power of Sauron?

I fear for the future of our world, Gandalf. If the Dark Lord's power is growing, if his influence is spreading, what hope is there for us? Are we doomed to walk in darkness, forever bound to the will of Sauron?

(round 6) Gandalf: Yes, at present, until all else is conquered. The Elves may fear the Dark Lord, and they may fly before him, but never again will they listen to him or serve him. And here in Rivendell there live still some of his chief foes: the Elven-wise, lords of the Eldar from beyond the furthest seas.
